moments.title: Networks and connections
moments.text: The presenter introduces graph theory through connected towns and networks.

moments.title: Vertices, edges and degree
moments.text: Locations are vertices; links are edges. Degree counts incident edges in the illustrated graph.

moments.title: Directed and undirected
moments.text: Arrows restrict allowed travel direction; an undirected edge can be traversed either way.

moments.title: Weights
moments.text: A weighted edge can represent a quantity such as travel time.

moments.title: Connected graphs
moments.text: In an undirected connected graph, every vertex is reachable from every other.

moments.title: Complete graphs
moments.text: A complete graph joins every pair of distinct vertices directly.

moments.title: Subgraphs and route terminology
moments.text: The presenter introduces subgraphs and names several types of route.

moments.title: Adjacency tables and matrices
moments.text: The video introduces row-to-column adjacency information and matrix powers.

moments.title: Minimum spanning trees
moments.text: The presenter introduces connecting all vertices at minimum total weight.

moments.title: Edge and vertex routing
moments.text: The video contrasts route problems involving edges and vertices; see the corrections beside the video.

moments.title: Review
moments.text: The video closes with a high-level review and practice recommendation.

notes.text: The video introduces graph terminology but does not fully develop all required definitions, directed in/out degree, strong connectivity or trees. These are explained on the page.

notes.title: Routing terminology later in the video
notes.text: The video describes the Chinese postman problem as traversing every edge exactly once. In general, a shortest closed postman route must traverse every edge at least once and may need repeated edges. A classical Hamiltonian cycle visits each vertex once before returning to its start.
notes.write: Check whether the task covers edges or vertices and whether repetition is permitted.

ican.text: I can model a context using vertices and edges and interpret edge weights.
I can distinguish simple, complete, directed, weighted and connected graphs.
I can calculate degree, in-degree and out-degree, including loops when permitted.
I can identify a subgraph or tree and check whether a directed graph is strongly connected.
I can apply the degree sum rule and distinguish graph structure from a particular drawing.

ku.text: A graph has a set of vertices and edges. Adjacent vertices are joined by an edge; adjacent edges share a vertex. A graph models a relationship, and the interpretation of a vertex or edge depends on the context.

An undirected edge can be traversed in either direction; a directed edge has an arrow from its tail to its head. A weight may record cost, distance or time. A weight is not automatically a count of edges or a probability.
A simple graph has no loops and no parallel edges. A loop joins a vertex to itself; parallel edges are distinct edges joining the same pair. State when loops or parallel edges are allowed.

The degree of a vertex in an undirected graph is the number of incident edge ends: an ordinary incident edge contributes one and a loop contributes two. The sum of degrees is $2|E|$, including loops counted this way.

In a directed graph, in-degree counts incoming edge ends and out-degree counts outgoing edge ends. A directed loop contributes one to each. The sum of in-degrees and the sum of out-degrees both equal the number of directed edges.

An undirected graph is connected if every pair of vertices is joined by a path. A directed graph is strongly connected if every vertex can reach every other following arrow directions. Ignoring arrows can hide a failure of strong connectivity.
The complete simple undirected graph $K_n$ joins every pair of distinct vertices exactly once. Each vertex has degree $n-1$, and the total number of edges is $n(n-1)/2$.

A subgraph uses a subset of the original vertices and edges, with each selected edge retaining its endpoints. An induced subgraph on chosen vertices includes every original edge between those vertices.
A tree is a connected undirected graph with no cycles. A tree with $n$ vertices has $n-1$ edges; connectedness is essential when using this property to check a candidate.
Graphs that look different in a drawing can have the same connections. An edge crossing is not automatically a vertex unless it is marked or specified as one.

misc.weak: A loop contributes one to the degree of an undirected vertex.
misc.better: It contributes two edge ends, so it contributes two to the degree.

misc.weak: A strongly connected directed graph only needs every vertex to have an incoming and outgoing edge.
misc.better: Every vertex must be reachable from every other following the arrows. Degree conditions alone are not enough.
Connected means reachable by a path; complete means each distinct pair is joined by an edge.

misc.weak: A graph with $n-1$ edges must be a tree.
misc.better: It must also be connected; otherwise a cycle and a disconnected vertex may coexist.

misc.weak: A road crossing on a diagram is necessarily a graph vertex.
misc.better: It is a vertex only when the model indicates a connection there.

formula.text: Undirected degree sum: $\sum_{v\in V}\deg(v)=2|E|$, counting a loop twice.
A complete simple graph $K_n$ has $n(n-1)/2$ edges; a tree with $n$ vertices has $n-1$ edges.

worked.prompt: An undirected simple network has vertices $A,B,C,D,E$ and edges $AB,AC,BC,CD,DE,EA$. Each edge represents a two-way route.

parts.label: a
parts.q: Find every vertex degree and verify the degree sum.
parts.a: The degrees are $\deg A=3$, $\deg B=2$, $\deg C=3$, $\deg D=2$ and $\deg E=2$. Their sum is $12=2(6)$, consistent with six edges.

parts.label: b
parts.q: Is the network connected or complete? Explain.
parts.a: It is connected: $A-B-C-D-E$ reaches every vertex. It is not complete because, for example, there is no edge $AD$.

parts.label: c
parts.q: Give a spanning tree and explain why it is a tree.
parts.a: Choose edges $AB,BC,CD,DE$. They connect all five vertices in a chain and have no cycle, so they form a spanning tree. There are $5-1=4$ edges.

parts.label: d
parts.q: How many additional edges are needed to make this graph complete?
parts.a: $K_5$ has $5(4)/2=10$ edges. The network has six, so four more are needed: $AD,BD,BE,CE$.

parts.label: e
parts.q: Separately, a directed graph has arcs $A\to B$, $B\to C$, $C\to A$, $C\to D$ and $D\to C$. Find the in-degree and out-degree of $C$ and decide whether it is strongly connected.
parts.a: For $C$, incoming arcs are $B\to C$ and $D\to C$, so in-degree is $2$; outgoing arcs are $C\to A$ and $C\to D$, so out-degree is $2$. It is strongly connected: from any vertex one can reach $C$, and from $C$ one can reach every vertex following arrows.

kq.q: Why does an undirected loop count twice in degree?
kq.model: Both ends of the edge are incident to the same vertex. Counting edge ends therefore counts the loop twice.

kq.q: Why is a complete graph connected when it has at least one vertex?
kq.model: Every distinct pair has a direct edge, so every vertex can reach every other.

kq.q: Why is strong connectivity stronger than ignoring arrow directions?
kq.model: A route that exists after removing arrow restrictions might be impossible to follow in one or both directions in the directed graph.

kq.q: Why does a spanning tree omit cycles?
kq.model: A tree is connected and acyclic. Retaining a cycle would violate its definition, even if the graph still spans all vertices.
